title: 1 Kings 15:1–8
context: The narrative alternates between Judah and Israel, dating each reign by the other kingdom’s king. Abijam of Judah reigns three years and walks in his father’s sins, yet the LORD preserves a lamp in Jerusalem for David’s sake. Second Chronicles 13 gives a fuller and more positive account of this king (there called Abijah) and names his mother differently; the relationship between the two accounts is discussed below.

verses.text: Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijam begins to reign in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year. Arminian readers note that each new king receives a fresh opportunity to lead the people back to God, so the evaluations that follow describe real choices rather than predetermined outcomes.
verses.reformedNotes: The synchronism with Jeroboam ties Judah’s history to Israel’s, a reminder that both kingdoms remain under one Lord. Reformed readers see the steady framework of reigns as an expression of God’s orderly rule over the history of his people.

verses.text: He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijam reigns only three years, and his mother is named as Maacah daughter of Abishalom. Arminian readers note how brief his reign is, and how little of it Kings counts as worth recording beyond his spiritual record.
verses.reformedNotes: The same Maacah is later named as Asa’s mother (15:10), and 2 Chronicles 13:2 gives Abijam’s mother a different name. Many interpreters suggest mother can mean grandmother or queen mother, but the relationships are uncertain, and Reformed readers usually leave the question open.

verses.text: He walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him; and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijam walks in his father’s sins, and his heart is not wholly devoted to the LORD as David’s was. Arminian readers stress that the comparison holds him responsible for the direction of his own heart, not merely for inherited patterns.
verses.reformedNotes: Second Chronicles 13 records a speech by this king condemning Jeroboam’s idolatry, a more favorable picture. Reformed readers commonly hold that the two accounts emphasize different aspects of his reign, while acknowledging that their relationship is debated.

verses.text: Nevertheless for David’s sake, the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him and to establish Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: For David’s sake, the LORD gives Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to David extending mercy to an unworthy descendant, giving the dynasty time and opportunity to return.
verses.reformedNotes: The lamp recalls God’s promise to David (11:36; 2 Samuel 7). Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness preserving the line despite the king’s failure. The site already treats the Davidic covenant as shared ground, and this verse fits that reading.

verses.text: because David did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, and didn’t turn away from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
verses.arminianNotes: David did right except in the matter of Uriah. Arminian readers note that Scripture names David’s sin plainly even while honoring him, a reminder that faithfulness overall does not erase serious failure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s great sin is acknowledged without canceling his standing as the model king. The existing box at 2 Samuel 12:13 already discusses how the traditions read a believer’s grave fall, and that discussion applies here.

verses.text: Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes: The war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continues throughout his life. Arminian readers see division between the kingdoms as the bitter fruit of earlier choices by Solomon, Rehoboam, and Jeroboam.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers recall that the division came from the LORD as judgment on Solomon’s idolatry (11:11-13; 12:24), yet the ongoing hostility shows the brokenness that judgment left behind.

verses.text: The rest of the acts of Abijam, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijam’s other acts are left to the chronicles of Judah’s kings, and the war with Jeroboam continues. Arminian readers note that Kings is selective, telling us what matters for covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: The reference to another record shows the writer drawing on sources now lost. Reformed readers see the inspired author choosing what to include so that the theological purpose of the history stands out.

verses.text: Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in David’s city; and Asa his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijam dies and is buried in David’s city, and Asa succeeds him. Arminian readers note that the next king inherits a troubled legacy but also a real chance to change course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuation of David’s line as the lamp of 15:4 in action. God preserves the dynasty from generation to generation, whatever the faithfulness of each king.
